en: The Śramaṇa Ji composed this treatise.
From "If there is only consciousness" up to "there are three natures," the commentary states:
although there are seven verses that explain external objections, they are divided into two parts. The first two verses answer the objection that there is only consciousness.
The latter five verses respond to the objection that [the teaching of] "consciousness-only" contradicts the sūtras;
this latter section contains two parts.
The first three verses explain the objection that the three natures are not established in the absence of objects;
the final two verses explain the objection that the three absences of nature are not established in the presence of consciousness. Within this initial section, there are four parts.
First, the general question;
second, the brief answer;
third, the inquiry.
There are four explanations;
this is the first. The intent of the present objection is as follows:
If external phenomena do not exist apart from internal consciousness, then...
If there were only one nature, it would not be appropriate to speak of three;
since the sūtra speaks of three, it is not merely consciousness-only.
[End of] Treatise.
"One should know that the three natures are likewise not separate from consciousness.
Commentary: This is a brief answer.
It is not that because three natures are taught it follows that there is not merely consciousness-only;
for these three are taught precisely as being inseparable from consciousness.
— Treatise.
Why is this so? The commentary states:
This is an objection raised by an outsider.
What is the reason why these three are not separate from consciousness? The treatise states in verse:
"Up to the point where one does not fail to see this or that."
The commentary states:
The following is the extensive response.
Within the verse, there are three parts.
The first two verses distinguish the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The latter verse clarifies the identity and difference of these three in its first three lines;

the fourth line clarifies that at the time of internal realization, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are realized and perceived sequentially.
Within the first two verses,
the first verse explains the first nature (parikalpita-svabhāva),
and the subsequent half-verse explains the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
The following half-verse explains the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The remainder of the text is easily understood.
In the subsequent commentary, the text is divided into two parts.
First, the explanation of the verse text;
second, the explanation by way of various categories.
Within the explanation of the root verse, there are further two divisions.
First, the individual verses of the *Kārikā* are explained;
subsequently, from "The meaning intended herein is as follows" onwards,
the general meaning of the verses is interpreted to provide a concluding answer to the question posed.
The detailed explanation of the verses is further divided into three parts.
First, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are distinguished;
second, their non-differentiation into a single meaning is distinguished.
The subsequent analysis of the sequence of realization and views consists of three sections for the separate explanation of the three natures,
or alternatively, two.
First, the first verse is explained regarding the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, the latter half of the verse explains the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
because it is explained in relation to the former, these two are combined as one.
The final half-verse explains the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The first section is divided into two parts.
The first explains only the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
the second explains it in conjunction with the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Treatise:
It is called "thorough conceptualization" (*parikalpa*) because it universally and exhaustively calculates and discriminates.
Commentary: [As follows].
This explains two interpretations regarding what is grasped;
these are precisely the interpretations previously offered by Nanda and others,
which explain the two characters "parikalpa" (imagined) in the first line of the verse.
The character "zhu" (周) explains the sense of pervasion (*pari*);
the character "du" (度) explains the sense of conceptualization (*vika*).
Only the sixth consciousness is capable of pervasive conceptualization.
Since the seventh consciousness and its associates belong to this same category, they are also termed "parikalpa" (imaginative construction).
However, they can only be called "kalpa" (construction) and not "parikalpa" (universal construction).
Now, we shall rely on the correct doctrine.
From this, one should formulate a fourfold analysis (catuṣkoṭi).
There are those that are pervasive but not conceptualized;
namely, all untainted (anāsrava) consciousnesses.
While tainted wholesome consciousnesses and the like are able to take objects extensively and universally,
they do not involve conceptual clinging;
whereas other [consciousnesses] may involve clinging but are not universal.
This refers to the seventh consciousness with outflows (*sāsrava-vijñāna*),
which is both pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and conceited (*manana*).
It refers to the sixth consciousness and its associates, such as the afflicted grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) that are associated with outflows.
There are those that are neither pervasive nor conceptualized;
namely, the five contaminated sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) and the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*), etc.
Question: Why is this pervasive imagination (parikalpa) called "this and that" (tattad)?
Treatise:
Because its categories are manifold, extending up to unreal conceptualization (abhūtaparikalpa).
The commentary states:
Because these types of mental reckonings are numerous— such as two or three—
they shall be understood in detail below.
It is said to be "this" or "that.
What is its essence?
It is the false discrimination that is capable of pervasive conceptualization.
This refers to all minds that give rise to the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) based upon the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra*).
In order to explain the second phrase, one first interprets the preceding phrase,
as well as the word "due to" (*yō*).
Treatise:
It is precisely by means of those respective [cognitions] reaching the objects that are the basis of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpya-vastu*).
Commentary states:
Due to false conceptualization, one universally imagines various objects of imagination.
"Objects" refers to their essence;
that is, the grasping that arises from the imagining mind.
What is the nature of this? The treatise states:
it refers to that which is falsely grasped as the self-nature and its specific distinctions.
The commentary states:
This nature is precisely that which is falsely grasped as all objects of meaning,
such as the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus).
Regarding these two— phenomena and the self— their intrinsic nature and their specific distinctions do not exist as entities external to the mind;
rather, they arise from the fact that the mind,
which possesses the capacity for conceptualization, imagines the existence of such things.
The term "universal imagination" (*parikalpa*) in the preceding phrase indicates the essence of the mind and so forth that perform the imagining;
it reveals the nature of those phenomena by way of their mode of activity as universal imagination.
In the second phrase, the term "parikalpa" (imagining) refers to the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of the mind that performs imagining; previously,
it was by means of this aspect that the essence of those phenomena was brought forth.
Later, the error of giving rise to conceptual constructions based on the characteristics [of phenomena] is clarified. Question:

Since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these conceptually constructed phenomena does not exist, why are they called "entities" (*vastu*) and "varieties" (*nānātva*)? Answer: It is in accordance with the mind that performs the conceptualization.
Therefore, it is called a "thing" (*vastu*).
Because the mind has many varieties, it is said to have various natures; yet it is not itself manifold.
Furthermore, even that which is reckoned as a non-existent phenomenon (*abhāva*) may be termed a "thing."
Because both existence and non-existence are termed "things" (*vastu*).
As for the term "various," it refers to how the falsely discriminating mind that performs pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) conceives of this non-existent thing.
Because mental states also possess various characteristics. [The] Treatise [states]:
"From this false attachment up to the intrinsic nature of that which is grasped..."
The commentary states:
This explains the third phrase.
It means that the falsely grasped external phenomena, self, intrinsic nature, and distinct entities referred to in this second phrase do not exist.
Because things such as a tortoise’s hair have no inherent existence whatsoever,
they are collectively termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
— Treatise.
"Thus, because its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is ultimately unapprehendable.
Commentary: This refers to the fourth line of the verse.
Thus, the third phrase refers to the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
which is entirely non-existent;
it is called "entirely non-existent" because not even the slightest thing can be found therein.
Because the phenomena of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) may exist to a slight degree.
How is it known that they do not exist?
Because they cannot be found when subjected to subtle investigation through both reasoning (yukti) and scripture (āgama).
As for the principles and teachings cited previously in the seventh fascicle and elsewhere,
this constitutes one reversal that merely explains the first nature;
below follows the second master’s explanation.
First, there is a brief explanation of the initial verse alone;
later, there is an extensive treatment in contrast with the *paratantra*,
which also explains the subsequent half-verse.
Treatise:
Alternatively, the first phrase reveals the consciousness that performs universal imagination (*parikalpa*).
Commentary states:
The meaning is the same as before. The treatise states:
The second phrase indicates the object that is the basis of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpya-viṣaya*).
The commentary states:
The locus of attachment upon which it relies differs from that of the former masters.
This is stated from the perspective of principle;
it applies to both the dependent and the perfected natures,
as will become clear below.
However, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other such texts speak only of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
because it is the basis upon which one stands and because it is somewhat proximate [to the perfected nature].
Because it is within the realm of ordinary beings and is easy to understand,
its principle is established as being consistent with the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
Treatise:
The latter half of the section only begins to explain [the argument] up to the point where [the object] cannot be apprehended.
Commentary: [As follows].
The latter half of the verse consists of the following two lines,
which formally set forth the meaning that the nature of parikalpita-parikalpita (the imagined) does not exist;
for its non-existence has already been extensively demonstrated in the seventh fascicle above.
However, as stated in the fourth and fifth fascicles of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, that which is the "universal conceptualizer" (*parikalpaka*) corresponds to this first phrase,
while that which is the "object of universal conceptualization" (*parikalpya*) corresponds to this second phrase.
The nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) is thus established;
this refers to the second half of the verse above,
which merely reiterates the object of attachment mentioned in the first half of the verse.
From here below, the first verse is explained in detail;
furthermore, based on the *paratantra-svabhāva*,
the three [natures] are explained extensively in three sections.
However, since the third phrase is explained in conjunction with the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
and it has already been stated that the first phrase refers to the universal imputer (*parikalpaka*),
the treatise next poses the question:
Treatise.
First, what is the nature of the universal imagination (*parikalpa*)?
The commentary states:
This is the introductory question.
Below, first the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) is explained in detail,
and subsequently each specific instance is explained in detail.
Treatise:
There is an interpretation that the eight consciousnesses all possess the capacity for pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*).
Commentary states:
These [masters], such as Sthiramati and others,
maintain that [grasping] pervades all three natures;
there is no contaminated mind that is not grasping.
5. The eight consciousnesses possess only the grasping of dharmas;
the seventh possesses only the grasping of a person;
the sixth pertains to both types.
Treatise:
Because its intrinsic nature is false discrimination.
Commentary: [As follows:]
If there were a tainted mind that, like an untainted one, did not give rise to grasping,
then it should not be called false discrimination.
If a non-grasping mind were to be called false discrimination, [it would be illogical].
In that case, the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) should also be called a mind of false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
By this same principle, it is clarified that all tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*) are capable of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*).
This is evident in the texts of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Madhyānta-vibhāga*.
It is said that all eight consciousnesses are false discrimination (*vikalpa*). According to the treatise,
this is because they all manifest as resembling the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
The commentary states:
Within the holy teachings, it is said that "grasping" refers to the grasping of the subject (grāhaka) and the object (grāhya).
Since all contaminated minds manifest with the appearance of both subject and object, they all possess grasping.
A mind that does not grasp is not called "grasping," yet a mind that lacks grasping still appears as the two types of grasping;
this is stated in all the sūtras and śāstras.
In the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, it is stated as follows: [The treatise says...]
It is said that the *ālaya* serves as the objective condition (*ālambana*).
The commentary states:
[it refers to] the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the false attachment to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is grasped.
This refers to the seeds of the grasping mind and so forth.
The fifty-first chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, as well as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and other texts,
state that the ālayavijñāna takes as its object the seeds of false attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
If there is a contaminated mind that does not involve grasping,
and there are contaminated seeds which the eighth consciousness does not take as its object,
why does the treatise state that the eighth consciousness takes delusive seeds as its object?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 76, as well as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*,
state that the eighth [consciousness] has the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the object-condition, the name-condition, and the conceptualization-condition as its objects.
Fascicle 51 states that it takes the seeds of the pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*) as its condition.
Therefore, the seeds of parikalpita (imagined nature) pervade all contaminated minds;
that is, masters such as Anvaya and others maintain that even within virtuous minds and so forth, there exists attachment to dharmas.
Below this is the second [section], concerning masters such as Dharmapāla.
Treatise:
There is an interpretation that the sixth [consciousness] up to this point is capable of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*).
Commentary states:
The following text has three parts:
first, the statement of the thesis;
second, the establishment of proof.
This is the first of three contradictions;
it is entirely not the five or eight consciousnesses.
Nor is it all minds,
because only those who cling to a self and phenomena are able to perform such reckoning. Why is this so?
Treatise:
It is taught that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*).
Commentary: [As follows].
There are ten proofs for this;
the ten instances of the character "hence" (故) are they.
If one can calculate the mind as penetrating through the eight consciousnesses, [then...]
How is it that the fourth chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* speaks only of the manas?

Question: Since the seventh consciousness is also capable of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), why does that treatise mention only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and not the seventh?
Is it that the seventh [consciousness] is incapable?
Since the seventh consciousness is indeed capable yet not mentioned,
it is made clear that the fifth and eighth consciousnesses are likewise capable yet not mentioned.
Treatise:
Because the mind (*manas*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are termed "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).
Commentary states:
The seventh is named *manas*.
When combined with the sixth consciousness,
they are collectively termed "mental consciousness" (*mano-vijñāna*), which has already been explained.
Who says it is not taught?
For example, within the Hīnayāna, regarding karma and the paths of karma (*karmapatha*),
volition (*cetanā*) is considered karma but not a path.
The three factors beginning with greed are paths but not karma;
the two factors of body and speech are both karma and paths.
Taken collectively, they are simply termed "paths of karma."
The seventh is called the mind (*manas*);
the sixth is called mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Taken together, they are termed "mental consciousness."
Therefore, the aforementioned objection does not apply. An-hui and others ask:

"Why do you not allow that only the sixth consciousness is capable of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), while the other seven consciousnesses, though also capable of conceptualizing, are not?"
It is not that it is not universally conceptualized; it is simply not mentioned in the *Saṃgrahaṇī*. It is not that others do not conceptualize it.
Both commentaries on the two treatises, in the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, provide this interpretation.
It is said that the sixth consciousness is able to engage in pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*);
its nature accords with that name,
whereas the others do not, and therefore that treatise does not mention them.
Furthermore, just as you speak of karma and the paths of karma together, I do so as well.
The seventh is called "mind" (manas);
the five and the eight are called "consciousness" (vijñāna).
The sixth is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
What fault is there in summarizing them collectively and calling it "mental consciousness"?
Therefore, it is known that all eight consciousnesses are capable of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*). According to the treatise,
this is because the conceptualizing discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) is capable of pervasive conceptualization.
The commentary states:
Since the five [sensory consciousnesses] and the eight [mental consciousnesses] lack discursive deliberation (*vitarka*),
it is clear that they are non-conceptual and do not give rise to grasping.
The fourth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states:
"It should be known that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the universal conceptualizer (*parikalpaka*),
because it possesses discrimination (*savikalpa*)."
Thus, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) functions with infinite modes of activity;
because it universally conceptualizes and discriminates all things, it is called "universal imagination" (*parikalpa*).
This is not the case for the five sensory consciousnesses or the eighth consciousness, as they are incapable of such universal conceptualization.
If that were so, the seventh [consciousness] would be unable to conceive of [the self] universally and thus should not be included here; however,
this statement is not intended to mean that.
Among the three types of discrimination,
it is the *vikalpa-vikalpa* (conceptual discrimination) that is capable of performing the seven kinds of discrimination regarding characteristics, up to and including non-defiled [discrimination];
this is because the five sensory consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness do not possess this capacity.
Because the seventh consciousness possesses *vikalpa* (conceptualization), it can be subsumed under this [category];
the fifth and eighth are not so.
As Vasubandhu says:
The mental consciousness is characterized by conceptualization because it is intermingled with the conceptualizations of discernment (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).
Discernment is that which calculates and determines.
"It is not its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because it also exists in others.
This is the correct interpretation. The former master said:

The five and eight types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that involve discursive calculation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) and coarse, high-level grasping of characteristics (*nimitta*) do not exist [in the formless realm].

However, those that are subtle—namely, the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) and spontaneous conceptualization (*anubhava-vikalpa*)—are said to exist in both the five and eight [classes of consciousness].
How could this principle be at fault?
Although the *Saṃgrahaṇī* speaks in terms of coarse conceptualization and discrimination, it does not explicitly state that there are five or eight [consciousnesses].
In reality, both the fifth and eighth consciousnesses are truly capable of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

Furthermore, because all eight consciousnesses are distinguished from uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds, it is said that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) alone possesses the capacity for conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
This does not mean that only the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are intended.
Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "It is solely by virtue of this category [of consciousness] that one is able to engage in pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpa*)."
Without discriminating which [of these] it is,
because there are those who lack the nature [to understand] and those with partial understanding of the root treatise,
he employs qualifying terms such as "manifestation" (*pradarśana*) and so forth to distinguish them.
What contradiction is there in this?
Later, it is challenged as follows: The Treatise says:
Since those who grasp at a self and dharmas must necessarily possess wisdom (*prajñā*), [the author] states:
"The five and eight consciousnesses do not constantly coexist with wisdom; how, then, could they possibly harbor such grasping?"
The former master said: "If one calculates that wisdom (*prajñā*) is coarse when it is the five [mental factors] and eight [mental factors], then even subtle [wisdom] exists.
If this is so, why is the mental factor of wisdom not considered a universal (*sarvatraga*)?
Thus says the treatise.
Because the two types of grasping must necessarily coexist with ignorance.
The commentary states:
The two graspings—of self and of phenomena—must necessarily coexist with ignorance.
Because there is ignorance within the non-virtuous mind,
and because that [ignorance] is diametrically opposed to the nature and characteristics of the wholesome root of non-delusion.
What fault is there in the statement of that former teacher?
According to my own Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) investigation, vitarka and vicāra arise simultaneously;
it is permissible to allow that their nature is such that they may coexist.
However, the natures of wholesome consciousness and ignorance are mutually contradictory.
Treatise:
It is not said that ignorance possesses a wholesome nature.
Commentary: [As follows].
Since treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* do not state this,
we shall cite those texts when discussing the latter two obstacles.
How can it be said that ignorance exists within a wholesome mind?
If he were to say that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are called unwholesome (*akuśala*),
on the grounds that they are designated as such because their characteristics are slight compared to wholesome conduct (*kuśalacaryā*),
[the treatise] states:
Because ignorance (*moha*) and non-ignorance (*amoha*), and so forth, are not associated (*asaṃprayukta*).
The commentary states:
because mutually contradictory phenomena are not associated.
Just as lack of shame (*ahrīkya*) and shame (*hrī*) cannot arise simultaneously,
the same principle should apply to delusion (*moha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*), and so forth.
If it is claimed that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are unwholesome (*akuśala*), [this would be incorrect].
Non-delusion and delusion are not said to be associated.
That which has a subtle characteristic of delusion is called non-delusion.
[Abhidharma] Śāstra.
This is because one does not perceive any grasping that leads [to the view of] emptiness.
The commentary states:
If the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) necessarily arises as either of the two types of contemplation on emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
If a contaminated mind necessarily involves attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
then how can the wisdom of application (*prayogajñāna*), which likewise possesses such attachment,
lead to the manifestation of the wisdom of emptiness?
It is not because fire is produced by being led by water,
nor is it because darkness serves as a precursor for the arising of light.
Treatise.
Because the grasping at existence and the realization of non-existence do not arise simultaneously.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, the preparatory mind that accords with the holy teachings and performs the contemplation of the emptiness of self and phenomena is called "realization of non-existence."
Since the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha) is termed "grasping at existence," how could such grasping co-arise with the wisdom that realizes non-existence?
Since those two do not arise simultaneously,
it is clear that the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) does not possess attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
Thus says the treatise.
Because there has never been a case of grasping that is not capable of perfuming.
[The commentary] states:
Furthermore, if all contaminated minds possess the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
The mind that clings to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) must necessarily possess a potent force;
therefore, the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) should also be capable of perfuming (*vāsana*),
because the outflowing mind (*sāsrava-citta*) possesses such functional efficacy.
Just as with the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth,
you maintain that the eighth consciousness is also not a perfuming agent,
because this retributive consciousness lacks functional efficacy.
Since no mind characterized by grasping or functional power is observed that could act as a perfumer,
the eighth consciousness should likewise be a perfumer;
otherwise, it would contradict inferential reasoning (*anumāna*).
If that is so, why do the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*,
the *Madhyānta-vibhāga* (first fascicle),
and other texts state that the three realms and the eight consciousnesses are all false conceptualizations?
The *Xiányán shìlùn* (Exposition of the Manifestation of the Teachings), chapter sixteen, states the same:
"Defiled minds and so forth are false conceptualizations (*abhūta-parikalpa*)."
The commentary states:
There are three points in the following text that resolve contradictions;
this is the first resolution.
To address this, it is said:
although one practices the contemplation of the two emptinesses during the preceding stages and so forth, these are merely provisional signs;
they do not equal the realization of the true principle through uncontaminated wisdom.
All eight consciousnesses are termed false discrimination (*vikalpa*).
Not all that is not false discrimination is a mind of grasping (*abhiniveśa-citta*).
If there were any outflowing (*sāsrava*) minds that were not grasping, [it would contradict the principle].
How can it be said that there is the manifestation of the two grasping marks?
The *Madhyāntavibhāga* states that the false mind and mental factors manifest as resembling these two marks.
All possess grasping. The treatise states:
although they appear to be objects of apprehension, they nonetheless possess grasping.
The commentary states:
In this assembly, there are two contradictions in the second [section],
which constitutes one assembly.
The two difficulties:
[the difficulty regarding] this assembly and the first difficulty concerning all tainted minds (*sāsrava-citta*).
Although it appears as if the aspects of the grasped and the grasper are manifest,
it is not all minds that engage in pervasive conceptualization;
for there are also dependent-originated minds that are wholesome or indeterminate.
Although the two types of grasping appear, they do not all arise as attachments;
nor does the mere appearance of these two imply that everything is capable of being a universal conceptualizer (*parikalpa*).
This is because there exists a mind in which the images of the two types of grasping appear through constructive discrimination (*vikalpa*) that is capable of universal conceptualization.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga* bases its discussion solely upon the six and seven consciousnesses.
If everything resembling the two types of grasping were considered "clinging," then it would follow that uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind would also possess clinging, which is not the case.
The post-attainment uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of all bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles possesses the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*);
it is associated with attachment. This is stated in the seventh [chapter] on the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).
It is simply stated that the untainted [cognition] of the two vehicles involves grasping;
according to the *Viṃśatikā-bhāṣya*,
the subsequently attained cognition of Bodhisattvas also involves grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
This differs from the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*.
That text speaks only of the outflows-free states of the two vehicles as being possessed of grasping;
this text merely states that the Buddha is without [grasping], without explicitly indicating that others also possess it.
Treatise:
Because the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom must necessarily involve grasping.
Commentary states:
He challenges the previous master’s statement, saying:
"The Buddha must possess grasping,
because he has the two types of apprehension of signs."
Because all bodhisattvas manifest two aspects;
if one were to argue that the Tathāgata’s subsequently attained wisdom lacks these two aspects,
it would contradict the sacred teachings and constitute a fallacy.
Furthermore, the aspect of being without images contradicts the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and its commentary;
for the sūtra states that the Buddha’s wisdom reaches [the state] of being like a mirror and so forth.
